title: Salesforce OAuth Token Security Breach Mitigation for APAC Teams
summary: Salesforce OAuth token security breach mitigation for APAC CRM teams: scope the exposure, harden connected apps, and meet PDPC, OAIC and PCPD notification clocks.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** Salesforce OAuth token breaches exploit third-party connected apps, not Salesforce itself. Mitigate by inventorying all OAuth grants, preserving Event Monitoring logs before revoking, setting finite refresh token lifetimes, restricting apps to admin-approved users and vendor IP ranges, and scoping integrations to least privilege.


---


The uncomfortable truth about Salesforce OAuth token security breach mitigation is that your Salesforce org was probably never the weak point. The connected app was. Every revenue intelligence, competitive intelligence, chat, and customer success tool your sales team installed over the last three years holds a refresh token that behaves like a permanent, MFA-exempt key to your CRM — and most of those vendors are smaller, younger, and less hardened than Salesforce itself.


*Related reading:*[Salesforce CRM OAuth Security Incident Response: APAC Playbook](https://branch8.com/posts/salesforce-crm-oauth-security-incident-response-apac-playbook)


I run operations for a business that supports global beauty and luxury brands out of Hong Kong, and I think about this the way I used to think about squad depth: your defence is only as strong as your weakest starter. In 2025, the weakest starter in most APAC Salesforce deployments was a third-party app nobody could name an owner for.

## The attack pattern shifted from your org to your app marketplace


Two incidents defined the year. In August 2025, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published research on UNC6395, a threat actor that obtained OAuth tokens associated with the Salesloft Drift application and used them to systematically export data from Salesforce instances belonging to hundreds of organisations, according to GTIG's 2025 threat intelligence report. Salesforce and Salesloft revoked all active access and refresh tokens for the Drift application on 20 August 2025, as Arctic Wolf documented in its own advisory. The attackers weren't exploiting a Salesforce vulnerability. They were using valid credentials, through a sanctioned integration, over the API.


Then in November 2025, Salesforce issued a security advisory regarding unusual activity involving Gainsight-published applications connected to Salesforce and revoked active tokens for those apps while investigating. Gainsight subsequently published a post-incident write-up identifying OAuth token longevity as a root cause it needed to fix.


Separately, GTIG tracked UNC6040 — a vishing-led campaign where attackers called employees, talked them into authorising a modified Data Loader-style connected app, and pulled data out directly, according to GTIG's advisory on the campaign. Same outcome, different entry point: a legitimate OAuth grant, obtained socially.


The pattern across all three: no exploit, no malware, no MFA prompt. A token is a bearer credential. Whoever holds it is you.


## Why APAC deployments carry more exposure than headquarters assumes


Most multinational Salesforce estates I've seen in Hong Kong, Singapore, and Taiwan were architected in San Francisco or London and extended into Asia by regional teams under revenue pressure. That produces three structural problems.


**App sprawl happens at the edge.** The global security team governs the core org. The APAC sales team installs the chat widget, the CI tool, and the meeting recorder because the quarter is closing. Regional admins frequently hold "Manage Connected Apps" without being part of any security review cadence.


**Data residency assumptions break on export.** A token-based bulk export doesn't respect your internal rule that Greater China customer records stay in a specific instance. It takes whatever the token's scope allows. If your org holds Hong Kong, Taiwan, Japan, and Australia customer data in one instance with shared sharing rules, a single compromised integration is a multi-jurisdiction notification event.


**Notification clocks differ by market.** Australia's Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, administered by the OAIC, requires assessment of a suspected eligible breach within 30 days and notification as soon as practicable, according to the OAIC's published guidance. Singapore's PDPC requires notification of notifiable breaches within three calendar days of assessment, per the PDPC's data breach notification framework. Hong Kong's PCPD operates a voluntary notification regime under the PDPO, while the HKMA expects authorised institutions to report material incidents promptly under its supervisory framework. If you operate across all four, your incident response runbook has four different timers running simultaneously — and the slowest one dictates how fast your forensics need to produce answers.


That is the real cost. Not the breach. The reconstruction.

## Establish whether you were actually affected before you rotate anything


Resist the urge to mass-revoke on day one of an advisory. You will take sales operations offline and destroy the evidence you need for regulatory notification. Sequence it: scope, then contain, then rotate.


Start with what tokens exist. In Salesforce, the` OauthToken` object gives you per-user grants:


```text
1  SELECT   Id  ,   AppName  ,     User  .  Username  ,     User  .  Profile  .  Name  ,     2         LastUsedDate  ,   UseCount  ,   DeleteToken    3   FROM   OauthToken    4   ORDER     BY   LastUsedDate   DESC
```


Run it from the CLI so you have a timestamped artefact, not a screenshot:


```text
1  sf data query \    2    --query "SELECT Id, AppName, User.Username, LastUsedDate, UseCount FROM OauthToken ORDER BY LastUsedDate DESC" \    3    --target-org prod-apac \    4    --result-format csv > oauth-inventory-$(date +%F).csv
```


Then pull the integration-level view:


```text
1  sf data query \    2    --query "SELECT Id, Name, CreatedDate, CreatedBy.Name, OptionsAllowAdminApprovedUsersOnly FROM ConnectedApplication" \    3    --target-org prod-apac
```


For evidence of what a token actually did, Event Monitoring is the only reliable source. If you have Shield or the Event Monitoring add-on:


```text
1  sf data query \    2    --query "SELECT Id, EventType, LogDate, LogFileLength FROM EventLogFile WHERE EventType IN ('API','BulkApi','RestApi','ApiTotalUsage') AND LogDate = LAST_N_DAYS:30" \    3    --target-org prod-apac
```


What you're hunting in those logs: unusual` USER_AGENT` values, bulk query jobs against` Account` ,` Contact` ,` Opportunity` , or` Case` with row counts far above the integration's normal pattern, and source IPs outside the vendor's published ranges. GTIG's UNC6395 reporting noted the actor queried objects including Cases and Accounts and attempted to clean up by deleting query jobs — which is why the Setup Audit Trail and log file retention window matter more than the dashboard.


One thing teams consistently miss: tokens are a trailing indicator. Check what left, not just what connected.


## Treat every credential the integration could have seen as burned


Here is the second-order risk that caught a lot of organisations in the Drift incident. GTIG reported that the actor searched exported data for secrets — AWS access keys, Snowflake tokens, passwords — sitting in Salesforce Case records and support ticket text. Customers paste credentials into support cases. Your sales engineers paste API keys into Opportunity notes. That content is now in an exfiltrated CSV.


So the rotation scope is not "the Salesforce token." It is:


- The connected app's OAuth tokens and any client secrets
- Any API key, service account, or password that appears in free-text fields the token could read
- Session tokens for integrated systems that share SSO with the compromised path
- Anything your team has ever committed to a repository — run` gitleaks detect` or` trufflehog filesystem` across your Salesforce metadata repos and any internal tooling, because the "Salesforce OAuth token security breach mitigation github" search pattern exists for a reason: hardcoded tokens in` .env` files and sandbox config are a standing exposure independent of any vendor incident


Then search your own org for the mess:


```text
1  SELECT   Id  ,   CaseNumber  ,   Subject   FROM     Case     2   WHERE   Description   LIKE     '%AKIA%'     3       OR   Description   LIKE     '%password%'     4       OR   Description   LIKE     '%api_key%'
```


Run it. The result count is usually sobering, and it tells you how much credential rotation you owe downstream customers — which in regulated APAC markets may itself be a notifiable event.

## A connected app policy worth enforcing


Mitigation that lasts is configuration, not a memo. These are the controls that change the economics of a stolen token, in rough order of payoff.


### Expire refresh tokens


The default "Refresh Token is valid until revoked" setting is why a token stolen in May still works in November. Set an expiry. In Setup, under the connected app's OAuth policies, choose "Immediately expire refresh token" for interactive apps or a fixed window for server-to-server integrations. Gainsight itself named token longevity as the root cause it addressed — take the hint.


### Restrict permitted users to admin-approved


Setting` OptionsAllowAdminApprovedUsersOnly = true` means a user cannot self-authorise an app via a phishing or vishing flow. This is the single control that would have blunted the UNC6040 Data Loader campaign. It costs you an approval step per integration.


### Enforce IP restrictions per connected app


Most SaaS vendors publish egress IP ranges. Bind the app to them. If the token is used from an unexpected ASN — a common pattern in these campaigns was access via commercial VPN and hosting infrastructure — the call fails.


### Scope to least privilege, then verify


An integration that needs read access to Opportunities does not need` full` or` api` scope across every object. Over-scoping is the amplifier that turns a vendor incident into a full CRM export. Audit the permission set assigned to each integration user, not just the OAuth scope string.


### Deploy a Transaction Security Policy on bulk export


Event Monitoring plus Transaction Security lets you block or alert on large data exports in real time. An Apex condition builder policy on` ReportEvent` or API-based` DataExport` volume gives you a circuit breaker rather than a post-mortem.


### Run integrations through a dedicated, monitored user


Never let an integration ride on a named admin's grant. Separate integration users give you clean attribution in` EventLogFile` , a single revocation point, and no collateral damage when a person leaves the company.


## What vendor due diligence should actually ask for


I manage vendors for a living, and procurement security questionnaires are mostly theatre. Three questions separate a hardened vendor from a liability:


1. **"What is your refresh token lifetime against our org, and can we set it?"** If the answer is "valid until revoked, and no," you are accepting their breach as your breach, indefinitely.
2. **"Which objects and fields does your integration read, and will you accept a scoped permission set rather than a system administrator profile?"** Vendors who insist on broad access usually haven't done the work to need less.
3. **"What is your notification SLA to us, in hours, for a suspected token compromise — and do you support our regulators' timelines?"** A vendor that notifies in five days has made your three-day PDPC clock impossible.


Add a contractual right to receive log extracts. In both 2025 incidents, customers depended entirely on the vendor's forensic timeline to scope their own notifications.


One pattern from our own implementation work: a Greater China retail group running Salesforce alongside a marketing automation stack had eleven connected apps in production and documented owners for four. The remediation wasn't technical — it was an operational register with a named owner, a renewal date, and a quarterly review tied to the same cadence as their vendor contracts. Unowned integrations are the actual vulnerability. Everything else is downstream of that.

## Build the muscle memory before you need it


Treat this like pre-season. The teams that handled the Drift and Gainsight advisories well had three things ready: an inventory they trusted, a revocation runbook they'd rehearsed, and a regulatory contact list per jurisdiction.


A workable quarterly drill:


- Pull the` OauthToken` and` ConnectedApplication` inventory and diff it against last quarter. Investigate every addition.
- Revoke one non-critical integration in a full sandbox and time how long restoration takes. That number is your real downtime cost during an incident, and it's usually worse than people guess.
- Walk the notification decision tree for a hypothetical export of 50,000 APAC customer records. Who decides? Who drafts the PDPC, OAIC, and PCPD communications? Who tells the Japanese and Korean distributors?


The cost of running this drill is a few hours per quarter. The cost of not running it is discovering your dependency map during a live incident, across five time zones, with a three-day clock.


## What to do Monday morning


**1. Export your connected app inventory and assign an owner to every row.** Run the` sf data query` against` OauthToken` and` ConnectedApplication` above, drop it in a shared sheet, and put a human name next to each app by end of week. Anything with no owner and no login in 90 days gets revoked.


**2. Change the refresh token policy on your three highest-scope integrations.** Pick the apps with` api` or` full` scope and set a finite refresh token lifetime plus admin-approved users only. Do it in sandbox first; the breakage is usually a webhook, not the whole integration.


**3. Search your org for credentials in free text.** Run the` Case` and` Opportunity` description queries, count the hits, and brief your support and sales leads on why pasting keys into a ticket is now a regulatory problem in four markets.


Salesforce OAuth token security breach mitigation is heading the same direction identity management did a decade ago: non-human identities will get the same lifecycle discipline — provisioning, rotation, attestation, de-provisioning — that we already apply to employees. Vendors are starting to ship shorter token lifetimes by default, and regulators across APAC are getting more specific about third-party risk in supervisory guidance. The organisations that will handle the next advisory in an afternoon rather than a fortnight are the ones building that register now, while nobody is shouting.
